subject: physics
title: Required practical: specific heat capacity
key_idea: To find a **specific heat capacity**, heat a known mass with an electric heater. Measure the energy supplied and the temperature change. Then use c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ). Insulating and stirring improve the result.

sections.heading: Specific heat capacity and its equation

blocks.text: This section covers what specific heat capacity means and how the equation links the quantities you measure.

items.meaning: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.

blocks.label: Change in thermal energy
where: ΔE = change in thermal energy, in joules (J)
c = specific heat capacity, in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J/kg °C)
Δθ = temperature change, in degrees Celsius (°C)

blocks.text: In the practical you measure ΔE, m and Δθ. Rearrange the equation to find c.

blocks.label: Specific heat capacity
where: c = specific heat capacity, in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J/kg °C)
ΔE = energy transferred to the substance, in joules (J)
Δθ = temperature rise, in degrees Celsius (°C)

items.text: A 0.50 kg metal block gains 11 500 J of energy and its temperature rises by 25 °C.

diagram.alt: Calculate the energy needed to warm some water by a given temperature rise.
diagram.question: Water has a mass of {m} kg. It is heated and its temperature rises by {dT} °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Calculate the energy transferred to the water.

items: Specific heat capacity is the energy to raise 1 kg by 1 °C.
ΔE = m × c × Δθ, with mass in kg and energy in J.
To find c, divide the energy by the mass and the temperature rise.

blocks.text: An electric heater transfers energy to a block of metal or to water. You measure three things: mass, energy transferred and temperature change.

items: Mass: use a balance. For water, measure the mass of the empty beaker, then the beaker with water, and subtract.
Energy transferred: use a joulemeter connected to the heater.
Temperature: use a thermometer to find the start and final temperatures.
Alternatively, find the energy from the potential difference, the current and the time on a stopwatch.
The electric heater does work. This is the energy that increases the thermal energy of the block or water.
Calculate the temperature change by subtraction.

diagram.alt: Put the steps for measuring specific heat capacity into order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps of the method in order.
steps: Measure the mass of the block or of the water with a balance.
Insulate the block or beaker, and put the heater and thermometer in place.
Measure the starting temperature and the starting joulemeter reading.
Switch on the heater so the temperature increases.
Switch off and read the joulemeter. The energy transferred is the final minus the starting reading.
Measure the highest temperature reached and work out the temperature change.
Calculate c using c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ).

items: Measure the mass, the energy transferred and the temperature change.
Use a balance, a joulemeter and a thermometer.
Use c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ) to calculate the result.

blocks.text: Some of the energy from the heater is wasted. These steps give a more accurate value of c.

items: Insulate the block or beaker, or add a lid. Less energy is wasted and the temperature rise is greater.
Stir the water so its temperature is even.
After switching off, keep watching the thermometer and record the highest temperature. Energy takes time to spread by conduction and convection.
Keep the heater fully in the water or block.
Insulation and a lid reduce wasted energy.
Stir, and record the highest temperature reached.

checks.q: State the three measurements needed to find the specific heat capacity of a metal block.
checks.a: The mass of the block, the energy transferred to it, and the temperature change.

checks.q: Why does wrapping the block in insulation make the value of specific heat capacity more accurate?
checks.a: Less energy is wasted, and the temperature increase of the block is greater.

checks.q: A 0.40 kg block gains 18 000 J of energy and its temperature rises by 50 °C. Calculate its specific heat capacity.

mistakes.wrong: Heat the block and measure the temperature rise with a thermometer.
mistakes.right: A top mark answer must describe all three measurements: the mass, the energy transferred and the temperature change.

mistakes.wrong: Measure the mass of the water.
mistakes.right: A top mark answer needs a clear method for the mass of water: mass of the empty beaker, mass of beaker and water, then subtract.

mistakes.wrong: The specific heat capacity found is 4400 J.
mistakes.right: The unit is J/kg °C. The unit has its own mark.

worked_example.question: A student carried out an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of water. The energy transferred to the water was 26 400 J. The mass of water was 0.20 kg. The temperature increase of the water was 30 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of water using the data from this experiment. Choose the unit from J/kg, J/kg °C and J/°C.
worked_example.tip: One mark each for the substitution, the rearrangement, the answer and the unit. A correct numerical answer of 4400 scores 3 marks.

exam_phrases: (measurement of) the energy supplied / from the heater
(continue to) observe temperatures after switching off
record the maximum / highest / peak temperature reached
reduce heat loss / insulate the beaker / add a cover

mistakes.wrong: Read the final temperature as soon as the heater is switched off.
mistakes.right: Stir the water, keep observing after switching off and record the highest temperature reached. Conduction and convection take time.

mistakes.wrong: To improve the experiment, take repeat readings or use a more accurate thermometer.
mistakes.right: Repeats and more accurate measurements are ignored. Say insulate the beaker, add a cover, use a stirrer or transfer the hot copper faster.
Amount is ignored. Say the mass or volume of the water.

worked_example.question: A student uses apparatus to determine the specific heat capacity of water. State the measurements needed to calculate the specific heat capacity of water.
answer_points: The energy supplied by the heater.
Detail of any of these, for example measure the temperature at the start and end, or take the start and end readings on the joulemeter.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each measurement and one mark for detail. Volume or weight of water is accepted. The word amount is ignored.

blocks.text: The practical also asks for a temperature-time graph for melting ice.

items: Heat ice and plot temperature against time.
The line is flat at 0 °C while the ice melts. This is a change of state, so the temperature does not change.
When all the ice has melted, the temperature of the water rises.
